title: Fugue in E minor
blurb: The only two-voice fugue in either book. With just one line above and one below, every entry, every episode and every crossing is unmistakable — the best place to start.

title: Fugue in C minor
blurb: The textbook fugue: three voices, a compact subject, one regular countersubject, and episodes spun from the subject's own tail. If you learn to hear one fugue, it is this one.

title: Fugue in D minor
blurb: A short, fast three-voice fugue whose subject Bach turns upside down halfway through. Switch on the entry brackets and watch the shape flip.

title: Fugue in F major
blurb: A dancing 3/8 fugue. The subject is long and almost entirely stepwise, so each voice reads as a clear melodic line rather than a knot of figuration.

title: Fugue in B-flat major
blurb: A cheerful three-voice fugue on an unusually long, leaping subject — nearly four bars of it — which leaves room for only a handful of entries.

title: Fugue in C major
blurb: Almost nothing but subject. Four voices, no regular countersubject, barely an episode — entry piles on entry in stretto until the piece is saturated with its own theme.

title: Fugue in G minor
blurb: Four voices, a short and sharply characterised subject, and a countersubject that sticks to it. A good demonstration of how much four-part texture changes the sound of a fugue.

title: Fugue in E major
blurb: Bach writing deliberately in the old style: long white notes, alla breve, four voices moving like a Renaissance motet. Counterpoint at its most transparent.

title: Contrapunctus I
blurb: The plainest possible statement of the greatest fugal project ever undertaken: four voices, one subject, no tricks. Everything else in the cycle is a variation on this.
